name: Bitter apple (colocynth, Citrullus colocynthis)
short: Case reports after eating the fruit: acute kidney injury, raised liver enzymes and low blood pressure in one man; bloody diarrhoea and colitis in others. Topical trial abstracts give no harms data.
text: Evidence of harm comes from case reports and small case series after eating colocynth fruit. A 64-year-old man who ate it to relieve constipation developed profuse bloody diarrhoea, vomiting of blood and altered consciousness within 2 hours, with low blood pressure, acute kidney injury and raised liver enzymes, and recovered fully with supportive care within 5 days. A series of three cases after ingestion for ritual purposes described toxic acute colitis with dysenteric diarrhoea, with biopsy changes that disappeared within 14 days (one of the three also had a Clostridium perfringens intestinal infection), and another report described five cases of toxicity with severe bloody diarrhoea seen over 2 years. A case report of a 4-year-old child given bitter apple by a grandmother for constipation describes haemorrhagic colitis, and adds that low blood sugar and raised liver enzymes have been associated with ingestion. In contrast, in a 2-month randomised placebo-controlled trial in 50 people with type 2 diabetes on standard antidiabetic therapy, 100 mg fruit capsules three times a day caused no notable gastrointestinal side effects and no significant changes in liver enzymes, urea or creatinine. For use on the skin, a 3-month randomised placebo-controlled trial of a topical formulation in 60 people with painful diabetic neuropathy listed reported adverse events as an outcome, and a 2-month pilot randomised trial of topical oil in 34 people with chemotherapy-induced neuropathy set out to evaluate safety, but neither abstract gives adverse-event results. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
